Despite the folder name suggesting JavaScript, this is actually a **Django (Python) web application** — a graph editor with an SVG-based JavaScript frontend. Here's the breakdown:

---

## Top-level directories

| Directory | Contents |
|---|---|
| `grapheditor/` | Django project config — `settings.py`, `urls.py`, `wsgi.py`, `asgi.py` |
| `graph/` | The single Django app (all application logic lives here) |
| `images/` | GIF/PNG screenshots used in the README |
| `.circleci/` | CI pipeline config |

---

## `graph/` — the main app (~10 Python source files + 1 big JS file)

| File/Dir | Role |
|---|---|
| `models.py` | One model: `Graph` (name + path to a JSON file on disk) |
| `views.py` | 14 HTTP handler functions — CRUD for graphs plus graph algorithm endpoints |
| `convertation.py` | Pure graph utility functions: adjacency matrix ↔ JSON, Hamiltonian cycle search, binary tree construction, edge geometry |
| `urls.py` | URL routing for the app |
| `migrations/` | Single initial DB migration |
| `static/graph/js/draw.js` | 1,656-line jQuery/SVG frontend — all canvas drawing, node/edge interaction, and AJAX calls to the backend |
| `static/graph/js/jquery-3.5.1.js` | Vendored jQuery |
| `static/graph/css/background.css` | Frontend styles |
| `templates/graph/background.xhtml` | The single HTML page served to users |
| `graphs/graph130.json` | Example saved graph (JSON format) |

---

## Key dependencies (`requirements.txt`)

- **Django 3.0.7** — web framework
- **NetworkX 2.4** — graph algorithms (tree detection, diameter, radius, centre, products)
- **NumPy / SciPy** — matrix operations for graph representation
- **Gunicorn + WhiteNoise** — production serving (deployed to Heroku, per `Procfile` + `runtime.txt`)

---

## How it works

The browser renders an SVG canvas (`draw.js`) where users draw nodes and edges interactively. On actions like "make tree" or "find Hamiltonian cycle", the frontend sends the graph as JSON to a Django endpoint, which converts it to a NumPy matrix, runs NetworkX algorithms, and returns the updated graph structure.

baseline.answer:
Now I have a complete picture of the stack. Here is the full call chain for the `save` operation, which is the most illustrative path — it crosses every I/O boundary. I'll also note where the other endpoints diverge.

---

## Call Chain: `save()` → SQLite + filesystem

```
Browser event
  └─ draw.js:31       $("#save").on("click", ...) fires save()

Layer 1 — Client serialization (draw.js)
  └─ draw.js:1311     save()
       └─ draw.js:1601  graphToJson(graph)
            Walks graph.nodes[] and graph.edges[], converting
            each DOM-backed object into a plain JS object.

Layer 2 — Network I/O (browser → Django)
  └─ draw.js:1313     $.ajax({ url: "/edit-graph/SAVE_GRAPH/", data: {...} })
            jQuery issues an HTTP GET with the serialized graph
            as query-string parameters.

Layer 3 — URL routing (Django)
  └─ grapheditor/urls.py:23   path('edit-graph/', include("graph.urls"))
  └─ graph/urls.py:12         path('SAVE_GRAPH/', views.save_graph)

Layer 4 — View / business logic (graph/views.py:40)
  └─ views.save_graph(request)
       ├─ request.GET.dict()          — parse query string
       ├─ Graph.objects.get(id=...)   — ORM SELECT (→ DB I/O)
       ├─ open(graph.path_to_graph, 'w')
       │    └─ json.dump(structure, f) — File I/O (writes JSON)
       └─ graph.save()                — ORM UPDATE (→ DB I/O)

Layer 5a — Django ORM (graph/models.py:7)
  └─ Graph model (CharField name, CharField path_to_graph)
       Translates .get() / .save() into SQL statements.

Layer 5b — SQLite (db.sqlite3)
  └─ SELECT / UPDATE on the graph_graph table.
```

---

## Where other endpoints diverge

| Endpoint | Extra layers |
|---|---|
| `NEW_GRAPH` (`views.py:22`) | ORM INSERT → `graph.save()`, then `open(...,'w')` to create an empty JSON file, then another `graph.save()` to persist the file path |
| `GET_GRAPH` (`views.py:56`) | ORM SELECT to look up `path_to_graph`, then `open()` + `json.load()` for file read |
| `SAVE_GRAPH` | (primary example above) |
| `IS_TREE`, `FIND_DIAMETER`, `FIND_RADIUS`, `FIND_CENTRE` | No file I/O — deserialize the graph sent in the request body → `convertation.to_matrix()` → `numpy.matrix` → `networkx` algorithm |
| `VECTOR_PRODUCT`, `CARTESIAN_PRODUCT` | ORM SELECT to get the second graph's file path, file read (`json.load`) for that graph, then `numpy` + `networkx` algebra — two I/O paths in one request |
| `DELETE_GRAPH` | ORM DELETE only — the JSON file on disk is **not** deleted (a latent bug) |

---

## Summary of intermediate layers

```
Browser DOM event
  → Client-side serialization (graphToJson)
    → jQuery $.ajax (HTTP network request)
      → Django URL router (grapheditor/urls.py → graph/urls.py)
        → View function (graph/views.py)
          ├─ Django ORM → SQLite (db.sqlite3)          [database I/O]
          └─ Python open() / json.dump/load            [file I/O]
              → graph/graphs/graph<id>.json
```

The architecture has no dedicated service layer or repository pattern — the view functions act as both controller and data-access layer, calling the ORM and filesystem directly. The only separation of concerns is `convertation.py`, which handles pure graph-math transformations (adjacency matrix ↔ JSON) without touching I/O itself.

## Call Chain: `new Calendar(events)` → DOM I/O

### Layer 0 — Entry point (`index.js:17`)
```
new Calendar(events)
```
The caller constructs the widget and hands it a raw event array (plain objects with Unix-ms timestamps).

---

### Layer 1 — Constructor orchestration (`calendar.js:4–13`)
```
Calendar.constructor(events)
  ├── _validateEvents(events)       // guards: throws if data is malformed
  ├── _parseEvents(events)          // data transformation
  ├── currentDate = new Date()      // reads system clock
  ├── _scrollListener()             // registers DOM event listener
  ├── _addHeaderButtonEventListeners()
  ├── renderAllDayRow()
  ├── renderCalendarBody()
  ├── renderCalendarHours()
  └── render()                      // kicks off the main render cycle
```

---

### Layer 2 — Public render cycle (`calendar.js:58–62`)
```
render()
  ├── setTitle()        // writes month/year text into #calendar-title
  ├── renderDays()      // writes the Mon–Sun header row
  └── renderEvents()    // the path that reaches the deepest I/O
```

---

### Layer 3 — Event rendering (`calendar.js:64–72`)
```
renderEvents()
  ├── _resetAllColumns()            // clears all .calendar-body-column innerHTML ← DOM write
  ├── events.filter(...)            // pure in-memory filter using _isExistInThisWeek()
  └── forEach → _renderEvent(event) // one call per visible event
```

---

### Layer 4 — Per-event rendering (`calendar.js:145–161`)
```
_renderEvent(event)
  ├── _getDaysAndHours(dateFrom, dateTo)   // computes which cells to fill
  ├── forEach slot:
  │     ├── _getCell(slot.day, slot.hour)  // DOM read: document.querySelector(...)
  │     ├── cell.querySelector(...)        // DOM read: duplicate-check
  │     ├── document.createElement('div') // DOM write: builds event element
  │     ├── _addClicklistenerToEvent()     // attaches click handler
  │     └── cell.appendChild(eventDiv)    // DOM write: inserts into grid
  └── _setEventStartEndSize(event)         // DOM read+write: adjusts pixel height/margin
```

---

### Layer 5 — Time-slot computation (`calendar.js:267–288`)
```
_getDaysAndHours(dateFrom, dateTo)
  └── _getHours(dateFrom, dateTo)
        ├── clamps dateFrom/dateTo to current week boundaries (_getMonday / _getSunday)
        └── getDaysAndHours(currentDateFrom, currentDateTo)   ← crosses module boundary
```

---

### Layer 6 — Lookup table resolution (`lookUpDaysHours.js:694–718`)
```
getDaysAndHours(startDate, endDate)
  ├── extracts startDay, startHour, endDay, endHour from Date objects
  ├── computes diffDays
  └── returns a slice (or concat) of lookUpObject[day]
        └── lookUpObject  ← static in-memory JSON table (the "data store")
```
`lookUpObject` is a pre-built 7×24 matrix of `{ day, hour }` structs embedded directly in the module. There is no network call, no file read at runtime — the data is bundled into the JS module at parse time.

---

### Layer 7 — DOM cell targeting (`calendar.js:242–244`)
```
_getCell(day, hour)
  └── document.querySelector(`#calendar-body-row-${hour}`)   // DOM read
        └── row.querySelector(`[data-day="${day}"]`)          // DOM read
```

---

| # | Layer | Location | Role |
|---|-------|----------|------|
| 0 | **Entry / caller** | `index.js:17` | Instantiates `Calendar` with raw event data |
| 1 | **Constructor** | `calendar.js:4` | Validates, parses, wires listeners, delegates to render |
| 2 | **Public render** | `calendar.js:58` | Top-level render orchestrator (`render`) |
| 3 | **Event render loop** | `calendar.js:64` | Filters events to the current week, iterates |
| 4 | **Per-event renderer** | `calendar.js:145` | Builds DOM nodes, places them in the grid |
| 5 | **Time-slot adapter** | `calendar.js:267–288` | Clamps dates to the visible week, delegates to lookup |
| 6 | **Lookup / data layer** | `lookUpDaysHours.js:694` | Resolves a date range to `{day, hour}` slots via static table |
| 7 | **DOM I/O** | `calendar.js:242` / throughout | `querySelector`, `appendChild`, `innerHTML` — the actual "I/O" boundary |
